analysis.one_liner: Raises corporate taxes up to 35% and shuts down offshore tax avoidance techniques.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would restore the old graduated corporate tax rates with a 35% top rate on income above $10 million, end the flat 21% rate. It would tax profits that U.S. companies book through foreign subsidiaries, stop companies from shifting interest deductions and other payments to low-tax countries, tighten the rules on corporate inversions so a company can't escape U.S. taxes by moving its headquarters on paper, and tax foreign corporations managed from the United States as domestic companies. It would also scale back the special deduction for income U.S. companies report as earned abroad and limit tax-avoidance routes through tax treaties.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, whose own taxes would not need to cover revenue the government currently does not collect from multinational corporations; small businesses that compete against large multinationals with lower effective tax rates; and U.S. residents who would stop subsidizing corporate tax planning with deficit spending.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers and domestic small businesses

how_it_helps.text: Restores graduated corporate rates reaching 35% on income over $10 million, so the largest corporations pay at higher rates than before the 2017 tax law, while smaller firms face lower rates under the 15% and 25% brackets [S2].

Treats as taxable 'subpart F' income all profits of controlled foreign corporations derived from any foreign country, ending the practice of parking passive or easily-shifted income in low-tax jurisdictions [S2].
Applies the foreign tax credit limitation country by country, so companies can no longer use credits from taxes paid in high-tax countries to shield income from low-tax countries [S2].
Repeals the 'check-the-box' rules for foreign entities with limited-liability owners and the look-thru rule for related-party foreign income, closing two well-known planning techniques [S2].
Limits interest deductions for members of large international financial reporting groups, curbing the practice of loading U.S. subsidiaries with related-party debt to reduce U.S. taxable income [S2].

Strengthens anti-inversion rules: a foreign company formed to acquire a U.S. company would be treated as domestic if 80% of its stock is held by former U.S. owners, and companies whose management and control occurs primarily in the United States would be taxed as domestic corporations [S2].

Tightens the base erosion and anti-abuse tax by lowering the taxpayer threshold from $500 million to $25 million in gross receipts and raising the rate from 10% to 12.5%, plus restoring the dual-capacity taxpayer rules that limit foreign tax credits for payments that are really fees for special economic benefits [S2].

Limits treaty benefits for deductible related-party payments and income attributed to permanent establishments in low-tax third countries, and repeals the foreign-derived intangible income deduction [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large U.S.-based multinational corporations and foreign multinationals operating in the U.S., which would face higher effective tax rates and lose access to offshore planning structures, inversion transactions, and treaty-based avoidance routes.

drawbacks.text: Raising the top corporate rate back to 35% reverses a rate reduction enacted with broad bipartisan support in 2017; opponents argued such rates push investment and headquarters decisions abroad, and this bill's own anti-inversion provisions respond to that concern [S2].

Several provisions would apply to U.S. income tax treaties 'without regard to any treaty obligation of the United States,' which could put the U.S. in conflict with its treaty partners and invite retaliation against U.S. companies operating abroad [S2].

A near-total rewrite of the international tax rules would take away planning flexibility that even tax-avoidance critics have not proposed eliminating wholesale, creating compliance costs and transition problems for companies with global operations [S2].
Higher corporate taxes can reduce shareholder returns and, at the margin, some investment or wages, though the incidence of corporate tax increases is debated among economists [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets real, well-documented avoidance channels, but its cost is steep: returning the top corporate rate to 35% and unilaterally overriding tax treaties goes far beyond what even sympathetic tax-policy experts have proposed, and without any co-sponsor or committee process there was never any refining of the tradeoffs. The strongest parts, like country-by-country foreign tax credit rules and tighter interest-deduction limits, overlap with internationally coordinated efforts; the most aggressive parts, like blanket subpart F taxation, would put U.S. companies at a disadvantage against foreign competitors.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2024, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on April 10, 2024 [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, its only committee action [S4].
No cosponsors joined the bill; the cosponsor list is empty [S3].
The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and the Congress ended January 3, 2025, without further action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large multinational corporations keep the current 21% corporate rate and all of the offshore tax planning structures, including the foreign-derived intangible income deduction, check-the-box planning, and treaty-based routes, that the bill would have eliminated.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave it its only advocacy in the chamber record; no other members joined him.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate colleagues
against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors, leaving the bill with no bipartisan or even Democratic-party support in the record.

against.name: Multinational corporate lobby
against.role: U.S.-based multinationals and their Washington representatives
against.what_they_did: Long opposed rollbacks of the 2017 international tax provisions and offshore planning rules; no organized support for this bill ever emerged in the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got far enough for a vote; its single sponsor is an independent who caucuses with Democrats, and no member of either party signed on.

industries.note: The bill would raise their top rate from 21% to 35% and close the offshore structures, interest-deduction strategies, and FDII deduction that reduce their effective tax rates. Higher effective rates on profitable multinationals shift more of the overall tax burden away from wage earners who would otherwise cover the difference.

industries.industry: Foreign multinationals operating in the U.S.
industries.note: Foreign companies managed from the U.S. or using treaty routes through third countries would be taxed as domestic companies or lose treaty benefits, leveling the field against U.S. competitors but raising their costs.

industries.industry: Corporate tax planning and advisory firms
industries.note: Repealing check-the-box, the look-thru rule, and FDII, and adding country-by-country credit limits, would eliminate many of the structures these firms sell to clients; the bill would shrink the market for cross-border tax engineering.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and mining companies with foreign operations
industries.note: The dual-capacity taxpayer rules would prevent these companies from treating payments to foreign governments that come with special economic benefits as fully creditable taxes, increasing their U.S. tax liability.

The graduated rate structure leaves smaller corporations in the 15% and 25% brackets, and small firms generally lack the offshore structures the bill targets; their tax burden would not rise while large competitors' would.
